references.text: Matthew's parallel passage in the Sermon on the Mount: 'For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same?' Here Jesus uses tax collectors as an example instead of sinners, but the point is identical – loving only those who return that love is no extraordinary virtue.

The following verses elaborate on the same principle: doing good to those who do good to you, and lending to those from whom you hope to receive back, grants no special grace – for even sinners do the same.

The preceding context where Jesus commands to love enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, and pray for those who mistreat you. Verse 32 serves as the rationale for why such radical love is necessary.

The conclusion of the passage: Love your enemies, do good, and lend without expecting anything in return. Then your reward will be great, and you will be children of the Most High – for he is kind to the ungrateful and the wicked. Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.

Peter poses a similar rhetorical question: 'For what credit is it if, when you sin and are beaten, you endure? But if when you do good and suffer, you endure, this is a gracious thing in the sight of God.' The same principle that requires more than simply repaying good with good.

Jesus' command to love enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be children of your Father in heaven, who causes his sun to rise on the evil and the good. Parallel to Luke's version of the same teaching passage.

Paul elaborates on radical love: Christ died for the ungodly and sinners while we were still enemies. God's love surpasses human logic of reciprocity – it is directed toward those who do not deserve it.
John exhorts mutual love and points out that God's love is the model: He loved us first, not because we loved him. This exemplary love calls believers to love beyond natural reciprocity.

The command 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself' from the Torah forms the basis for Jesus' teaching on love. Jesus challenges his listeners to go even further than this – to love also those who do not love in return.
